Clustered and stratified data

Source: vignettes/articles/clustering.Rmd
clustering.Rmd

bootmakr obtains its standard errors, confidence intervals and p-values by resampling the data. What it resamples is your decision, and it should follow one rule: resample the units that you would treat as independent when choosing standard errors for the regression itself. If you would cluster the standard errors by firm, resample firms.

Your regression would use Resample R Stata
heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors observations (nothing to add) (nothing to add)
standard errors clustered in one dimension whole clusters cluster = "firm" cluster(firm)
standard errors clustered in two dimensions each dimension and their intersection cluster = c("firm", "year") not available
a stratified sample within strata strata = "region" strata(region)
clusters sampled within strata clusters within strata cluster = "firm", strata = "region" cluster(firm) strata(region)

Observations or clusters

Without cluster, each bootstrap sample draws observations with replacement. This allows the error variance to differ across observations, the bootstrap counterpart of heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. It still assumes that observations are independent.

When observations come in groups (employees in firms, firm-years in firms, respondents in villages), that assumption fails, and the bootstrap must draw whole groups. The example of Get started shows what is at stake. The data are firm-years, about seven per firm, and whether the CEO belongs to the owning family varies mostly between firms rather than within them. Here is the same call twice, once resampling firm-years and once resampling firms.

library(bootmakr)
library(haven)

osf  <- "https://osf.io/download/stk7y/?view_only=885d1ed5498c4b3c8a1194882e468286"
chen <- read_dta(osf)

ceo.model <- lg_ceopay ~ owner_ceo + ceo_tenure + PA_nic3_med + ceo_edu_dummy +
  lg_sales + firm_age + promoters_pct + institutions_pct +
  factor(year) + factor(nic_code_1digit)

by.firm.year <- bootmakr(ceo.model, data = chen, treat = "owner_ceo",
                         benchmark_covariates = "firm_age",
                         seed = 123, progress = FALSE)

by.firm <- bootmakr(ceo.model, data = chen, treat = "owner_ceo",
                    benchmark_covariates = "firm_age", cluster = "co_code",
                    seed = 123, progress = FALSE)

rbind("firm-years" = by.firm.year$results,
      "firms"      = by.firm$results)[, c("estimate", "se", "ci_lower", "ci_upper", "pvalue")]
#>             estimate         se   ci_lower  ci_upper pvalue
#> firm-years 0.3031863 0.04804267 0.20705034 0.3975676  0.000
#> firms      0.3031863 0.10616636 0.07812096 0.4990174  0.006
global osf "https://osf.io/download/stk7y/?view_only=885d1ed5498c4b3c8a1194882e468286"
copy "$osf" "ceo_pay.dta", replace
use "ceo_pay.dta", clear
global controls "ceo_tenure PA_nic3_med ceo_edu_dummy lg_sales firm_age"
global controls "$controls promoters_pct institutions_pct i.year i.nic_code_1digit"
* firm-years resampled
quietly bootmakr lg_ceopay owner_ceo $controls, ///
    treat(owner_ceo) benchmark(firm_age) seed(123)
display "firm-years:  se = " %6.4f r(se) "   95% CI [" %6.4f r(ci_lower) ", " %6.4f r(ci_upper) "]   p = " %5.3f r(p)

* firms resampled
quietly bootmakr lg_ceopay owner_ceo $controls, ///
    treat(owner_ceo) benchmark(firm_age) cluster(co_code) seed(123)
display "firms:       se = " %6.4f r(se) "   95% CI [" %6.4f r(ci_lower) ", " %6.4f r(ci_upper) "]   p = " %5.3f r(p)
firm-years:  se = 0.0480   95% CI [0.2036, 0.4000]   p = 0.000

firms:       se = 0.1080   95% CI [0.0919, 0.5173]   p = 0.002

The adjusted estimate is the same in both rows, because it is computed from the original sample. Only its uncertainty changes, and it changes a lot: the standard error is 0.048 when firm-years are resampled and 0.106 when firms are, 2.2 times as large. Treating the firm-years as independent overstates how much information the data hold about family CEOs, in the bootstrap just as in the regression itself.

The cluster bootstrap needs a reasonable number of clusters, just as cluster-robust standard errors do. The usual guidance is a few dozen at the least, and more when clusters differ much in size (Cameron & Miller, 2015). With few or very unequal clusters its confidence intervals can be too narrow, and no number of replications repairs that. The simulations in Lonati and Wulff (2026) document how coverage depends on the number and balance of clusters.

Two cluster dimensions

Panel data are often clustered in two ways at once: observations of the same firm are related, and so are observations of the same year. In R, give cluster two variables. bootmakr then runs three bootstraps, one resampling each dimension and one resampling their intersection, and combines the three variances as Vfirm + Vyear − Vfirm×year, following Cameron, Gelbach, and Miller (2011).

To see it at work we simulate a small panel in which both the treatment and the error term have a firm component and a year component.

set.seed(2026)
firms <- 60
years <- 25
panel <- expand.grid(firm = seq_len(firms), year = seq_len(years))

by.firm <- function() rnorm(firms)[panel$firm]
by.year <- function() rnorm(years)[panel$year]

panel$x <- rnorm(nrow(panel))
panel$d <- 0.5 * panel$x + by.firm() + by.year() + rnorm(nrow(panel))
panel$y <- 0.3 * panel$d + 0.5 * panel$x + by.firm() + by.year() + rnorm(nrow(panel))
one.way <- bootmakr(y ~ d + x, data = panel, treat = "d",
                    benchmark_covariates = "x", cluster = "firm",
                    seed = 123, progress = FALSE)

two.way <- bootmakr(y ~ d + x, data = panel, treat = "d",
                    benchmark_covariates = "x", cluster = c("firm", "year"),
                    seed = 123, progress = FALSE)
two.way
#> 
#> Call:
#> bootmakr(formula = y ~ d + x, data = panel, treat = "d", benchmark_covariates = "x", 
#>     seed = 123, cluster = c("firm", "year"), progress = FALSE)
#> 
#> Bootstrap sensitivity analysis (1,000 reps per dimension, n = 1,500, two-way clusters: firm=60, year=25, intersection=1500)
#> Benchmark: x | kd = 1, ky = 1
#> 
#> Adjusted estimates (normal-approx 95% CI):
#>   Estimate Std. Err     2.5%    97.5% Pr(>|0|)   
#> d 0.262590 0.080215 0.105371 0.419809  0.00106 **
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
#> (H0: adjusted estimate = 0; SE = sqrt(V_G + V_H - V_GH), CI = est +/- z*SE, p = 2*(1 - Phi(|z|)))
#> 
#> Benchmark strength (descriptive: computed from the data, no standard errors involved)
#>                       Partial R2 |Partial r|
#> x with treatment | X      0.1355       0.368
#> x with outcome | D, X     0.0625       0.250
#> Implied strength of the omitted variable (sensemakr bounds):
#>           kd   ky R2dz.x R2yz.dx |r_dz.x| |r_yz.dx|
#> 1.00x x 1.00 1.00 0.1567  0.0915    0.396     0.303
#> (R2dz.x, R2yz.dx: partial R2 of the omitted variable with the treatment given the
#>  covariates, and with the outcome given treatment and covariates; |r| = square root,
#>  i.e. the partial-correlation scale of the ITCV. Descriptive only: independent of the
#>  variance estimator. No t-implied correlation or threshold is reported.)

Clustering by firm alone gives a standard error of 0.070. Allowing for the year dimension as well raises it to 0.080.

A few things differ from the one-way case.

  • The result is a variance, not a bootstrap distribution, so the confidence interval and the p-value use a normal approximation (estimate ± 1.96 standard errors) instead of percentiles. The output says so.
  • reps is the number of replications per bootstrap, so the run does three times the work.
  • The combined variance can come out negative in small samples. bootmakr then falls back on the larger of the two one-way variances and tells you.
  • A dimension with very few clusters, such as five years, cannot support cluster-robust inference of any kind. bootmakr warns when a dimension has fewer than ten.
  • The draws of the three bootstraps are kept in $boot_samples$G, $H and $GH.

Two-way clustering cannot be combined with strata, and it is not available in the Stata command.

Strata

If the sample was drawn separately within strata (regions, industries, size classes), the bootstrap should respect that: strata resamples within each stratum, so every bootstrap sample has the same number of units per stratum as the data. Combined with cluster, whole clusters are resampled within strata.

bootmakr(y ~ d + x1 + x2, data = dat, treat = "d",
         benchmark_covariates = "x1",
         cluster = "firm", strata = "region")
bootmakr y d x1 x2, treat(d) benchmark(x1) cluster(firm) strata(region)

References

Cameron, A. C., Gelbach, J. B., & Miller, D. L. (2011). Robust inference with multiway clustering. Journal of Business & Economic Statistics, 29(2), 238–249. https://doi.org/10.1198/jbes.2010.07136

Cameron, A. C., & Miller, D. L. (2015). A practitioner’s guide to cluster-robust inference. Journal of Human Resources, 50(2), 317–372. https://doi.org/10.3368/jhr.50.2.317

Chen, G., Chittoor, R., & Vissa, B. (2021). Does nepotism run in the family? CEO pay and pay-performance sensitivity in Indian family firms. Strategic Management Journal, 42(7), 1326–1343. https://doi.org/10.1002/smj.3263

Lonati, S., & Wulff, J. N. (2026). Why you should not use the ITCV with robust standard errors (and what to do instead). Working paper.
